note: Sets out external testing and study design choices in detail, which is the methodological backbone of a clinical AI audit.
title: Methods for Clinical Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Algorithms for Medical Diagnosis.

reading.body:
Clinical AI evaluation depends on testing algorithms on data from outside the setting where they were built, not on the data used to develop them.

The paper is a methods guide rather than a trial or a new algorithm. It organizes the design choices that determine whether a diagnostic AI study produces usable evidence: independent external testing, performance measures and their interpretation, and the distinction between paired designs, which compare conventional and AI-supported diagnosis, and parallel designs, which assess an intervention and include randomized trials. It also surveys reporting guidance, including resources listed by the EQUATOR Network.

For AI specifically, the constraint this describes is evidence rather than computation. A diagnostic model can be trained and deployed with the same hardware and power as any other software, so the scarce input is proof that it works outside its training setting. That is what hospitals and regulators need before letting a model influence patient decisions, and it is why the paper's subject is study design rather than model architecture.

The data does not say how often external testing is done in practice, whether it changes outcomes, or how any of this is regulated. It records a methods article, its journal, its year, and its citation count of 141. It covers evaluation of diagnostic algorithms in medicine and nothing about the compute, buildings, or power that sit behind those algorithms.

explain_beginner: This paper is a guide, not a new experiment. It explains how to judge whether an AI tool for diagnosing patients is ready for real care. The authors say testing only on the data used to build the tool is not enough. It should also be checked on separate data from other settings. The paper covers how to measure performance, how to compare usual care with care supported by AI, and how to design studies, including randomized trials. It also points to reporting standards. This matters because hospitals and regulators need reliable evidence before trusting AI with patient decisions.
explain_business: For executives, this paper offers a framework for deciding whether diagnostic AI is ready for practice. It says evidence from only one setting is not enough. Testing in another setting is needed. It also explains how to compare AI-supported care with usual care and when stronger designs, such as randomized trials, are appropriate. It points to reporting standards that make studies easier to audit. In practice, this informs decisions about funding a pilot, requesting outside testing, requiring a trial, or waiting. It helps leaders judge evidence quality before committing resources or changing how diagnosis is delivered.
explain_practitioner: This methods article reviews how to evaluate diagnostic AI before clinical adoption. It does not present a new algorithm or trial result. Instead, it organizes key design choices. It discusses why testing on independent data is important and how to do that well. It examines performance measures and plots, plus pitfalls in interpreting them. It separates paired designs, used mainly to compare conventional and AI-supported diagnosis, from parallel designs, used mainly to assess an intervention, especially randomized trials. It also surveys current reporting guidance, including resources listed by the EQUATOR Network. The main takeaway is that stronger methodological knowledge improves study design, execution, reporting, and critical review.
